summary: Analyzes how real TCP implementations handle the urgent mechanism and how middleboxes interfere with it. It updates RFC 793, RFC 1011 and RFC 1122 to match current practice and advises against relying on urgent data. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 9293.

eli5.summary: TCP has a way to flag a part of the data as urgent, like waving a flag in a queue. In practice people handle the flag differently, so this note says not to count on it.

subtitle: Clarifying the TCP urgent mechanism and warning against its use.

tldr.problem: TCP's urgent mechanism is poorly implemented and understood. Different operating systems handle urgent data differently, the RFC specifications themselves contained ambiguities, and middleboxes sometimes interfere with urgent indications, making them unreliable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that the urgent pointer should point to the sequence number following the urgent data (not the last byte of urgent data), and acknowledges that most implementations deliver the last byte of urgent data out-of-band rather than in-line as the spec intended. It updates RFC 793, RFC 1011, and RFC 1122 to match current practice.
tldr.outcome: New applications should not use the urgent mechanism due to its unreliability. Legacy applications that must use it should set SO_OOBINLINE and be prepared for the URG flag to be cleared by middleboxes.

today: RFC 6093 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 793, RFC 1011, and RFC 1122 to document current implementation practice. It is the de facto standard for how TCP urgent data is handled. The current TCP specification is RFC 9293.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
The original TCP specification (RFC 793) defined an urgent mechanism that allows the sender to mark a point in the data stream as urgent, signaling that the receiver should process urgent data at that point. The sender sets the URG flag in the TCP header and provides an urgent pointer value. However, RFC 793 had an ambiguity: it was unclear whether the urgent pointer pointed to the last byte of urgent data or to the byte immediately following it.

RFC 1122 formally clarified that the urgent pointer should point to the last byte of urgent data, but this clarification was never implemented in real TCP stacks. Every widely deployed TCP implementation instead follows RFC 793's original (incorrect) interpretation, where the urgent pointer points to the byte after the urgent data. Given this reality, RFC 6093 updates the specification to match the actual behavior of all known implementations, eliminating the discrepancy between the specification and practice.
sections.eli5: The original rule was unclear about what the urgent flag means. People fixed it, but real programs never followed the fix. This note says the rule should just match what everyone actually does.

sections.title: How Implementations Actually Work
sections.content:
The TCP specification states that urgent data should be delivered "in-line" with normal data, meaning an application reads it as part of the normal data stream. However, virtually all TCP implementations deliver the last byte of urgent data "out-of-band" using special system calls like recv(MSG_OOB) instead. This was never the intent of the IETF specification but has become standard practice.

Many implementations provide the SO_OOBINLINE socket option that changes urgent data to be delivered in-line, conforming to the spec. However, even this option is inconsistent across systems. Some operating systems like Linux provide the tcp_stdurg sysctl to interpret the urgent pointer according to RFC 1122, but this toggle works only for incoming packets, not outgoing ones, making interoperability within the same host unreliable.
sections.eli5: All programs deliver urgent bytes as special out-of-band data, even though the rule says they should be normal. Some offer a checkbox to follow the original rule, but that checkbox does not work consistently.

sections.title: Middleboxes and Unreliability
sections.content:
Middleboxes such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems have been designed to clear the urgent flag and set the urgent pointer to zero on packets they process. This was done to prevent NIDS (Network Intrusion Detection System) evasion techniques that exploit the ambiguous handling of urgent data. When a middlebox clears the URG flag, the urgent data becomes in-line data in the receive buffer, changing the application's behavior depending on whether the application uses MSG_OOB or SO_OOBINLINE.

This behavior means that an urgent data stream transmitted through the Internet cannot be relied upon to arrive at the receiving application with the urgent flag intact. The receiving application may see the data as urgent, as normal, or with packets reordered, depending on the implementation and the middleboxes along the path. This unreliability is a fundamental reason why applications should not depend on the urgent mechanism.
sections.eli5: Security devices sometimes turn off the urgent flag to stop attacks. This means an urgent message might arrive normal, confusing the application. You cannot count on urgent data getting through as urgent.

sections.title: Guidance for Applications
sections.content:
New applications should not use the TCP urgent mechanism. The inconsistencies in implementation, the ambiguities in the specifications (even after clarification), and the interference by middleboxes make urgent data unreliable. Applications that need to signal high-priority data should use an application-level mechanism rather than relying on TCP's urgent mechanism.

Legacy applications that do use the urgent mechanism MUST set the SO_OOBINLINE socket option to have urgent data delivered in-line, conforming to the IETF intent. Additionally, these applications must be designed to work correctly even if the URG flag is cleared by middleboxes, meaning the application should not rely on the urgent data arriving out-of-band. Applications like Telnet and FTP that historically relied on urgent indications may encounter difficulties in networks with aggressive middleboxes.
sections.eli5: New programs should not use urgent data. Old programs that do must set an option to receive urgent data like normal data, and must work even if it arrives normal anyway.
